lessons.title: Recognize an enclosed-space hazard
lessons.goal: Explain why the senses cannot establish that an atmosphere is safe.
notes: An enclosed space can have too little oxygen, too much oxygen, or harmful gases and vapours. A space that looks empty can still contain an atmosphere dangerous to life.
Smell is not a dependable atmosphere test. The space, its previous contents, connected systems and the intended work all belong in the assessment.
Entry depends on the ship’s authorized assessment, safeguards, suitable testing, communication and rescue arrangements. An introductory lesson cannot establish entry permission or universal limits.
lessons.scenario: A colleague says an empty tank must be safe because there is no smell. What information is missing?
lessons.takeaway: Appearance and smell cannot replace the entry assessment.

questions.stem: What does an absence of smell establish?
options: It does not establish a safe atmosphere
It proves adequate oxygen
It excludes toxic gases
questions.explanation: Some dangerous conditions cannot be detected by smell, and oxygen concentration is not established by the senses.

questions.stem: Which belongs in an entry assessment?
options: Only the space’s paint colour
Previous contents and connected systems
Only the person’s experience
questions.explanation: Past contents and connected systems can affect the hazards present; experience alone does not resolve them.

questions.stem: What is the status of this study lesson?
options: A replacement for the ship’s permit
Permission to make an unplanned rescue entry
Background learning, not entry authorization
questions.explanation: Actual entry and rescue arrangements require the ship’s approved procedures, authorization and trained response.

lessons.title: Make a useful watch handover
lessons.goal: Separate present condition, changes and unresolved items.
notes: A useful handover gives the incoming watch a clear operating picture. Organize it into current condition, significant changes and outstanding work or concerns.
Distinguish a measured observation from an assumption. Include the time and equipment identity when they matter; do not describe an unresolved defect as repaired.
Ask the incoming watch to confirm critical information and resolve uncertainty using the required records and handover arrangements. Department-specific duties remain part of the ship’s procedures.
lessons.scenario: An alarm has stopped, but the cause has not been identified. Prepare a handover sentence that preserves that uncertainty.
lessons.takeaway: An alarm clearing and a defect being resolved are different facts.

questions.stem: Which handover preserves an unresolved defect?
options: The equipment is repaired because the alarm stopped
The alarm cleared; the cause is still under investigation
There is nothing worth mentioning
questions.explanation: The first statement separates an observation from a conclusion that has not been established.

questions.stem: Which detail makes an unusual reading easier to investigate?
options: An unrelated personal opinion
A claim that readings never change
Equipment identity and observation time
questions.explanation: A reading needs context so the next watch can locate the equipment and compare observations.

questions.stem: What helps confirm a critical handover item?
options: A clear confirmation of the information received
Assuming silence means agreement
Leaving the incoming watch to guess
questions.explanation: Confirmation helps expose misunderstandings; it does not replace the required handover checks.

lessons.title: Build the lookout picture
lessons.goal: Recognize that a proper lookout uses appropriate available information.
notes: International Rule 5 describes a lookout using sight, hearing and available means appropriate to the conditions. The purpose includes appraising the situation and collision risk.
A radar display, visual observation or automatic identification message supplies part of the picture. Instrument limitations and the actual circumstances matter.

Repeated observations and clear reports help the bridge team understand change. Rule applicability, safe speed, risk assessment and avoiding action must be considered together; this introduction does not prescribe a manoeuvre.
lessons.scenario: A visual contact is not on the selected radar display. Does that observation justify ignoring it?
lessons.takeaway: Use observations together and investigate conflicting information.

questions.stem: What is the best response to conflicting visual and radar information?
options: Ignore the visual contact automatically
Assume the display is infallible
Investigate and combine appropriate available observations
questions.explanation: One source cannot automatically invalidate another; the limitations and context need appraisal.

questions.stem: Which senses are expressly relevant to Rule 5?
options: Sight and hearing
Smell and taste only
Hearing only
questions.explanation: The International rule includes sight and hearing, alongside appropriate available means.

questions.stem: Can this introductory lesson alone select a course alteration?
options: Yes; every contact requires the same turn
No; the encounter and applicable rules must be established
Yes; display colour determines the turn
questions.explanation: Collision-avoidance decisions depend on the full encounter, conditions and applicable rules.

lessons.title: Recognize mooring-line hazards
lessons.goal: Identify why changing loads require situational awareness.
notes: Mooring operations involve lines under tension, moving equipment and changing vessel movement. A line and its equipment must be understood as part of the complete arrangement.
A painted marking is not proof that every nearby position is safe. The line lead, loading, equipment condition and possible movement affect the hazard picture.

Know the assigned role, communication arrangements and designated safe positions in the ship’s plan. Report uncertainty and follow the responsible officer’s instructions; this lesson does not define a universal safe distance.
lessons.scenario: The lead of a mooring line changes during an operation. What must be reconsidered about the people nearby?
lessons.takeaway: Reassess the actual arrangement when conditions change.

questions.stem: What affects the mooring hazard picture?
options: Line lead, loading and possible movement
Only the colour of deck paint
Only whether the vessel is large
questions.explanation: The actual arrangement and changing forces matter; paint alone cannot describe all hazards.

questions.stem: What does a deck marking guarantee?
options: A permanent safe zone in every operation
It does not guarantee safety in every changing arrangement
That a line cannot move beyond it
questions.explanation: Hazards depend on the real line and equipment configuration, not solely on markings.

questions.stem: What should an unclear assigned role prompt?
options: An improvised role beside a loaded line
Silence to avoid delaying work
Clarification through the operation’s communication arrangements
questions.explanation: Clarifying responsibilities supports coordinated work; guessing adds uncertainty.

lessons.title: Understand lubrication and cooling
lessons.goal: Distinguish system purpose from equipment-specific operating limits.
notes: Lubrication and cooling are supporting systems with different jobs. Lubrication helps separate moving surfaces and manage wear; cooling transfers unwanted heat away from components.
The correct fluid specification and operating range depend on the engine and system design. A pressure or temperature value from a different installation is not automatically applicable.

Use the identified equipment’s approved documentation to interpret readings and alarms. Look at the complete operating picture, including load and trends, rather than inventing a universal normal value.
lessons.scenario: Two engines have different documented temperature ranges. Does one range establish that the other engine is faulty?
lessons.takeaway: Identify the engine and its approved limits before judging a reading.

questions.stem: Which is a primary purpose of cooling?
options: Replace all lubrication functions
Transfer unwanted heat away from components
Guarantee that every part stays at ambient temperature
questions.explanation: Cooling removes heat; it does not make operating equipment remain at ambient temperature or replace the lubrication system.

questions.stem: Where should the fluid specification come from?
options: A remembered value from another vessel
A colour match alone
The applicable engine and system documentation
questions.explanation: Specifications depend on the equipment and application; appearance alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: What improves interpretation of a reading?
options: Equipment identity, load, trend and applicable limits
One number without context
A universal value for every engine
questions.explanation: Readings need context and equipment-specific limits to support a useful assessment.

lessons.title: Report a changing machinery trend
lessons.goal: Describe evidence clearly without turning a symptom into a diagnosis.
notes: A trend describes how an observation changes over time. Record the parameter, equipment, units and times so the information can be compared.
A changing temperature is a symptom, not a confirmed diagnosis. Consider the associated operating conditions and report uncertainty instead of naming an unproven cause.
Follow the ship’s alarm, escalation and watchkeeping instructions. Review or study practice must not delay a required response to an actual alarm.
lessons.scenario: A cooling-water temperature has risen between rounds while load has also changed. Write an observation without claiming a cause.
lessons.takeaway: Report what changed, when it changed and what remains uncertain.

questions.stem: Which is an observation rather than an unproven diagnosis?
options: The heat exchanger has certainly failed
The sensor must be wrong
Temperature increased between the two recorded rounds
questions.explanation: The observation describes evidence; the other statements assert causes without establishing them.

questions.stem: What makes a trend record comparable?
options: Consistent parameter identity, units and times
Omitting equipment identity
Changing units without recording them
questions.explanation: A trend is useful only when the measurements and their context can be compared.

questions.stem: What governs a real alarm response?
options: Waiting until a study quiz is finished
The applicable onboard response and escalation procedures
The most convenient explanation
questions.explanation: Actual alarm response follows the ship’s arrangements and takes priority over learning activities.

lessons.title: Bulk cargo: start with cargo hazards
lessons.goal: Recognize that solid bulk cargoes have different hazards.
notes: Solid bulk cargo is carried unpackaged in quantity. Cargo distribution affects the vessel, and cargo properties can introduce stability, structural and chemical hazards.
The IMSBC framework addresses safe carriage of solid bulk cargoes through cargo information and applicable schedules. Looking similar does not establish that two cargoes have the same hazards.
Use the actual cargo declaration and applicable requirements. This overview does not determine moisture acceptability, loading limits or a cargo’s fitness for shipment.
lessons.scenario: Two visually similar bulk cargoes have different declarations. What should guide their assessment?
lessons.takeaway: Identify the actual cargo and its relevant information.

questions.stem: Which code addresses solid bulk cargo carriage?
options: IMSBC Code
IBC Code for every solid cargo
A passenger muster list
questions.explanation: The IMSBC Code is the relevant solid-bulk framework; the IBC Code concerns listed dangerous chemicals and noxious liquids in bulk.

questions.stem: Which can be a bulk cargo hazard?
options: Only the cargo’s colour
Improper distribution affecting structure or stability
Only delay to the voyage
questions.explanation: Cargo distribution and cargo-specific properties can affect safety, beyond commercial consequences.

questions.stem: Does visual similarity prove identical cargo hazards?
options: Yes; appearance is sufficient
Yes; all bulk cargoes behave alike
No; identify the cargo and applicable information
questions.explanation: Different cargoes can look alike while having different carriage hazards and requirements.

lessons.title: Containers: think packing and securing
lessons.goal: Distinguish cargo packing from securing the unit on the ship.
notes: Packing concerns the arrangement of cargo within a transport unit. Stowage and securing also concern how units are arranged and restrained aboard the vessel.
A closed container does not show that its contents are correctly packed. Similarly, an intact exterior is not proof that shipboard securing is complete.

Cargo information, the applicable securing arrangements and the vessel’s approved documentation serve different purposes. This overview does not specify lashing loads or replace a securing calculation.
lessons.scenario: A container looks undamaged. Which packing and shipboard-securing questions remain unanswered?
lessons.takeaway: An intact exterior does not establish packing or securing adequacy.

questions.stem: What does packing primarily address?
options: Only the ship’s route
Cargo arrangement within the transport unit
Only the colour of container markings
questions.explanation: Packing deals with contents and their arrangement; shipboard stowage and securing add further requirements.

questions.stem: What can an intact container exterior establish about its internal packing?
options: It proves every internal item is restrained
It removes the need for cargo information
It does not by itself establish correct packing
questions.explanation: The contents and internal restraint cannot be established solely from the exterior.

questions.stem: What should guide actual shipboard securing?
options: The applicable approved securing documentation
A universal lashing pattern from this quiz
Appearance alone
questions.explanation: Ship and cargo arrangements require the applicable securing instructions and calculations.

lessons.title: Oil tanker: connect safety and pollution prevention
lessons.goal: Recognize the role of cargo information and oil-pollution controls.
notes: Oil tanker work requires both safe handling and pollution prevention. Product properties and the ship’s arrangements influence the hazards and controls.
MARPOL Annex I addresses prevention of pollution by oil. It does not make a generic study note sufficient to authorize an actual discharge or cargo operation.

Understand which documents govern the intended operation and who is responsible. Use the actual cargo information and approved onboard procedures; no transfer or discharge limits are set in this lesson.
lessons.scenario: A colleague assumes all oil products need exactly the same handling. What information should be checked first?
lessons.takeaway: Treat actual cargo information and applicable procedures as essential.

questions.stem: Which MARPOL annex addresses oil pollution?
options: Annex V as the oil annex
Annex IV as the oil annex
Annex I
questions.explanation: MARPOL Annex I covers oil; Annex V addresses garbage and Annex IV addresses sewage.

questions.stem: Do all oil products necessarily have identical handling hazards?
options: No; actual product properties matter
Yes; the word oil proves identical behaviour
Yes; only the vessel’s name matters
questions.explanation: The product and the ship’s arrangements affect the hazard assessment.

questions.stem: Does knowing an annex title authorize a discharge?
options: Yes; any discharge is then permitted
No; the applicable requirements and authorization still apply
Yes; study completion replaces the rules
questions.explanation: General knowledge is not an authorization or evidence that discharge conditions have been met.

lessons.title: Chemical tanker: identify the product
lessons.goal: Explain why compatibility and product hazards need specific information.
notes: Chemical cargoes can have substantially different hazards. A trade name or similar appearance is not enough to establish compatibility or suitable protection.
The IBC Code provides a framework for safe bulk carriage of the listed dangerous chemicals and noxious liquid substances. Product hazards influence the required ship and equipment arrangements.
Use the actual cargo documentation and applicable approved instructions. This introduction cannot decide whether two cargoes may be mixed or share equipment.
lessons.scenario: Two clear liquids have different cargo names and hazard documentation. Can appearance establish compatibility?
lessons.takeaway: Identify the product before drawing a compatibility conclusion.

questions.stem: Which framework concerns listed dangerous chemical cargoes in bulk?
options: IBC Code
IMSBC as the liquid-chemical code
A generic engine manual
questions.explanation: The IBC Code addresses the specified chemical and noxious liquid bulk cargoes; IMSBC concerns solid bulk cargoes.

questions.stem: Does similar appearance establish chemical compatibility?
options: Yes; clear liquids are interchangeable
No; product-specific information is needed
Yes; odour alone establishes it
questions.explanation: Appearance and odour are insufficient to determine compatibility.

questions.stem: What should guide an actual compatibility decision?
options: A visual comparison alone
This introductory quiz alone
Applicable cargo information and approved procedures
questions.explanation: Compatibility requires the applicable product and system information, not a generalized study example.

lessons.title: LNG carrier: understand the barriers
lessons.goal: Recognize containment, monitoring and emergency functions.
notes: LNG is carried as a cryogenic liquid. Low temperature and released vapour introduce different hazards, so containment and protective arrangements matter.
The IGC framework addresses carriage of liquefied gases and protective design. Actual containment and cargo-system arrangements differ between ships.

Detection, alarm and shutdown are distinct functions. Acknowledging an alarm does not establish that its cause is removed. Use the approved procedures and assigned responsibilities for any actual response.
lessons.scenario: A gas alarm is acknowledged and the display becomes quiet. What has this action not established?
lessons.takeaway: Acknowledgement is not evidence that the underlying condition is safe.

questions.stem: Which code framework concerns liquefied gases carried in bulk?
options: IMSBC as the gas-carrier code
IGC Code
Only a container packing guide
questions.explanation: The IGC Code is the liquefied-gas carriage framework; applicability must be checked for the vessel.

questions.stem: What does acknowledging an alarm establish?
options: That the leak has stopped
That monitoring is no longer required
Acknowledgement, not removal of the underlying cause
questions.explanation: Acknowledgement changes the alarm interaction; it is not proof that the hazardous condition has been resolved.

questions.stem: Are every LNG ship’s cargo arrangements identical?
options: No; the actual vessel arrangement must be identified
Yes; every ship has identical containment
Yes; the same valve lineup applies everywhere
questions.explanation: Containment, machinery and control arrangements vary, requiring vessel-specific information.

lessons.title: LPG carrier: identify the carriage arrangement
lessons.goal: Recognize why cargo and containment details matter.
notes: Liquefied petroleum gas carriage involves cargo properties and a designed containment arrangement. Pressure and refrigeration features depend on the installation.
A gas-carrier label alone does not establish operating conditions or equipment. Identify the cargo and the actual vessel arrangement before interpreting information.
The IGC Code provides the relevant liquefied-gas framework subject to vessel applicability. This lesson gives no pressure settings, transfer sequence or instructions for a real cargo system.
lessons.scenario: A learner transfers a remembered pressure value from another gas carrier. What is missing before it can be used?
lessons.takeaway: The actual cargo, installation and approved operating information come first.

questions.stem: What establishes the relevant operating information?
options: The label gas carrier alone
A remembered value from any other ship
The actual cargo and approved vessel documentation
questions.explanation: Gas cargoes and their installations differ; the appropriate information must match the application.

questions.stem: Can another ship’s pressure setting be assumed correct?
options: No; it needs equipment and cargo-specific verification
Yes; every LPG system is identical
Yes; if it is easy to remember
questions.explanation: A remembered value does not establish applicability to this system.

questions.stem: Which framework is relevant to liquefied-gas bulk carriage?
options: IMSBC for every gas cargo
IGC Code subject to vessel applicability
A bulk-solid schedule alone
questions.explanation: The gas-carrier framework is IGC, with the applicable requirements depending on the ship.

lessons.title: Passenger and Ro-Ro: protect people and boundaries
lessons.goal: Recognize passenger movement and integrity as separate responsibilities.
notes: Passenger and Ro-Ro work adds particular demands for people, vehicle or cargo movement and the ship’s protective arrangements. Individual ships have different layouts and assigned duties.
SOLAS addresses subdivision, fire protection and life-saving arrangements. A route familiar from another vessel may not match the current ship’s escape and muster plan.
Use the actual muster duties and approved arrangements. Never infer that a door or boundary may be left open from a generalized lesson; its function and applicable instructions must be established.
lessons.scenario: You join a different vessel with unfamiliar routes and door arrangements. What must your familiarization establish?
lessons.takeaway: Learn this vessel’s routes, duties and protective arrangements.

questions.stem: What should guide personal emergency duties?
options: This vessel’s muster and familiarization arrangements
Only experience from the previous vessel
The shortest route remembered from another ship
questions.explanation: Emergency roles and routes must match the actual vessel and assigned organization.

questions.stem: Does this overview authorize leaving a protective boundary open?
options: Yes; passenger convenience always overrides it
No; its function and applicable instructions must be established
Yes; all ship doors serve the same purpose
questions.explanation: Protective boundaries have specific functions; generalized study cannot authorize changing their status.

questions.stem: Which convention covers the cited subdivision and life-saving framework?
options: Only a container packing guide
Only a cargo invoice
SOLAS
questions.explanation: SOLAS includes requirements for subdivision, fire protection and life-saving arrangements, subject to applicability.

lessons.title: Offshore: understand the service and interfaces
lessons.goal: Recognize why a vessel’s actual task shapes its hazards.
notes: Offshore vessels carry out different services. A supply, support or specialist task can create different interfaces between vessel, personnel, cargo and offshore installation.
IMO offshore-supply guidance recognizes unique service characteristics. That does not make every offshore vessel or operation identical, or establish qualification for station keeping or lifting.

Identify the operation, assigned role, communication and applicable procedures before evaluating a scenario. This introductory lesson provides no dynamic-positioning, lifting or personnel-transfer instructions.
lessons.scenario: Two offshore vessels have different service roles. Why should their work arrangements not be assumed identical?
lessons.takeaway: Start with the actual service and its interfaces.

questions.stem: What should be established before assessing an offshore work scenario?
options: Only the vessel’s paint scheme
The actual service, roles and operating interfaces
That every offshore vessel does the same work
questions.explanation: Service and interfaces determine relevant context; the vessel label alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Does this introduction establish DP competence?
options: Yes; reading a paragraph qualifies the learner
Yes; a quiz replaces practical assessment
No; specialist competence needs the appropriate training and assessment
questions.explanation: Introductory awareness is different from specialist operational competence.

questions.stem: What makes a communication plan relevant?
options: It matches the actual task and responsible parties
It is copied unchanged from any previous vessel
It names no responsibilities
questions.explanation: Task-specific responsibilities and interfaces make communication usable for the actual operation.
